connection: Session 24 established the real throw-vs-return rule. This session traces a real exception's full propagation path -- GetDuartion's InvalidOperationException, uncaught anywhere between ClockEntry and Program.cs -- and studies IDisposable/using through the real database connections Sessions 30-31's tests already open.
objectives: Trace GetDuartion's real InvalidOperationException from where it is thrown up through PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours to Program.cs, and identify that nothing in that path catches it.
Explain what 'unhandled exception' means concretely for this console app: the process terminates and prints a stack trace, since Program.cs never wraps its calls in try/catch.
Explain what using (or await using) guarantees for a SqliteConnection or PayrollDbContext, even if an exception is thrown partway through the code block.
Identify a real await using PayrollDbContext db = new(options); statement in the test suite and explain what would leak without it.

visuals.title: An exception propagates up, unchanged, until something catches it
visuals.explanation: GetDuartion throws inside ClockEntry; CalculateTotalHours does not catch it; Program.cs does not catch it either -- the exception reaches the very top of the call stack unmodified.

visuals.title: No catch means the process terminates
visuals.explanation: dotnet run for a console app with an unhandled exception prints the exception's stack trace to stderr and exits with a non-zero code -- there is no generic 'error page' the way a web app might have.

visuals.title: using guarantees Dispose runs, exception or not
visuals.explanation: await using SqliteConnection connection = new(...) ensures the connection is closed even if an exception is thrown between opening it and the end of the block.

visuals.title: IDisposable is a contract for releasing unmanaged resources
visuals.explanation: SqliteConnection and DbContext both implement IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable because they hold real, external resources (a database connection) that the garbage collector alone cannot reliably clean up promptly.

preQuiz.prompt: If GetDuartion throws InvalidOperationException on an open entry, and PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours never catches it, what happens when Program.cs calls CalculateTotalHours?
options: The exception propagates unchanged all the way out of CalculateTotalHours, out of Program.cs's top-level statements, and terminates the process with an unhandled-exception stack trace
The exception is silently swallowed and CalculateTotalHours returns 0
The compiler prevents this code from ever throwing
preQuiz.explanation: Nothing in the real call chain -- ClockEntry, PayrollService, or Program.cs -- catches this exception, so it propagates all the way to the runtime's default unhandled-exception behavior.

preQuiz.prompt: What does await using SqliteConnection connection = new(...) guarantee that a plain SqliteConnection connection = new(...) (without using) does not?
options: connection.DisposeAsync() runs automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown partway through -- releasing the underlying database connection either way
preQuiz.explanation: using (and await using) compiles to a try/finally under the hood -- Dispose/DisposeAsync is guaranteed to run in the finally, regardless of whether the try block completed normally or threw.

preQuiz.prompt: Why do SqliteConnection and DbContext implement IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable at all?
options: They hold real external resources (an open database connection) that need explicit, timely release -- the garbage collector would eventually clean them up, but not promptly or deterministically enough for a resource this expensive
IDisposable is required by every C# class
It is purely a style convention with no functional purpose
preQuiz.explanation: IDisposable exists specifically for exactly this category of resource -- something external to the .NET managed heap that benefits from prompt, deterministic release.

concept.title: Tracing GetDuartion's real, unhandled exception
paragraphs: The path is real and short: ClockEntry.GetDuartion throws InvalidOperationException("Employee has not clcoked out yet") if ClockOut is null; PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours calls .Sum(x => x.GetDuartion().TotalHours) with no try/catch around it; Program.cs calls CalculateTotalHours with no try/catch either.

This is not a bug this course is inventing -- it is the real, current shape of the codebase, verified by reading all three files. GetEmployeeClockEntries's real ClockOut != null filter is what normally prevents this from happening in practice, by excluding open entries before Sum ever sees them.

concept.title: An unhandled exception in a console app terminates the process
paragraphs: There is no global exception handler anywhere in PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App's real Program.cs. If an exception ever did reach it unhandled, .NET's default behavior for a console app is to print the exception type, message, and stack trace to stderr, then exit with a non-zero exit code.
This is different from what Session 34 will cover for the WebApi project: ASP.NET Core has its own exception-handling middleware pipeline that a console app's top-level statements simply do not have.
concept.code:
// No try/catch anywhere in the real Program.cs -- an exception here would terminate the process
var result = payrollService.CalculateTotalHours(1, DateTime.Today.AddHours(-4), DateTime.Now.AddHours(4));

concept.title: using/await using: Dispose runs no matter what
paragraphs: The real integration tests already do this: await using SqliteConnection connection = new("Data Source=:memory:"); and await using PayrollDbContext db = new(options); both guarantee the connection and context are disposed at the end of their block, exception or not.

Without using, an exception thrown between opening the connection and the end of the method would skip whatever cleanup code came after it -- leaving the connection open until the garbage collector eventually, non-deterministically, finalizes it.

lab.objective: Reproduce GetDuartion's real unhandled exception end to end, and confirm using/await using's guaranteed cleanup by deliberately throwing inside a using block.
lab.startingCondition: ClockEntry.GetDuartion, PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours, and the real SQLite-based integration tests already exist.
steps: Call CalculateTotalHours in a way that includes an open (not clocked out) entry in the date range, and confirm the real, unhandled InvalidOperationException propagates out of the call.
Wrap that same call in a try/catch in a throwaway test and confirm you can observe the exact real exception message.
Write a small test that opens a using SqliteConnection, throws an exception inside the block, and confirms (via a flag or mock) that Dispose still ran.
Explain, in writing, why GetEmployeeClockEntries's ClockOut != null filter is what normally prevents this exception from surfacing in ordinary use.
lab.expectedBehavior: The unhandled InvalidOperationException is reproduced and its exact message confirmed; the using-block test confirms Dispose runs even when an exception is thrown inside the block.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm GetDuartion's real, unhandled exception path.
Confirm PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours has no try/catch around its Sum call.
Add a test reproducing the real unhandled-exception path and a using-block Dispose guarantee test.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-24: teach exception propagation idisposable and using
review: GetDuartion's real exception path is traced through all three real files (ClockEntry, PayrollService, Program.cs), not asserted abstractly.
The console app's real lack of a global exception handler is contrasted honestly with what Session 34's WebApi will need.
using/await using's Dispose guarantee is demonstrated with a real, deliberately-throwing test, not just described.

postQuiz.prompt: Why doesn't GetEmployeeClockEntries's real filter (ClockOut != null) fully eliminate the possibility of GetDuartion throwing inside CalculateTotalHours?
options: It eliminates it for THAT specific call path -- but any other code that calls GetDuartion directly on an open ClockEntry (bypassing GetEmployeeClockEntries's filter) would still trigger the same real exception
It does fully eliminate the possibility everywhere in the codebase
GetDuartion cannot be called on an open entry -- the compiler prevents it
postQuiz.explanation: The filter protects one specific call path, not GetDuartion itself -- GetDuartion's own guard clause is what actually protects it universally, which is exactly why Session 7 studied that guard clause directly.

postQuiz.prompt: What would you need to add to Program.cs for an unhandled exception from CalculateTotalHours to be caught and handled gracefully instead of terminating the process?
options: A try/catch block around the call, or a broader pattern like a global unhandled-exception handler -- neither currently exists in the real Program.cs
async/await, since only asynchronous exceptions can be caught
postQuiz.explanation: This is a genuine, currently-true gap in the real console app -- there is no exception handling anywhere in Program.cs today.

postQuiz.prompt: If a using block's Dispose call itself throws an exception, what happens to an exception that was already being thrown from inside the block?
options: This is a genuinely subtle edge case (Dispose exceptions during unwinding) -- in the common case relevant to this codebase's SqliteConnection/DbContext usage, Dispose completing without its own exception is what actually happens, so the original exception propagates normally
The original exception is always silently discarded
The program always crashes immediately with no information
postQuiz.explanation: This session focuses on the common, real case (Dispose succeeding) rather than the rarer double-fault scenario -- worth naming as a known edge case without needing to solve it here.

reflections: Why does this session trace a real exception path instead of inventing a hypothetical one?
What would change about Program.cs's behavior if it wrapped its ClockIn/Clockout/CalculateTotalHours sequence in a single try/catch?
Where else in this codebase (beyond the SQLite tests) might a resource benefit from using/await using that doesn't currently have it?
whatBreaks: Calling GetDuartion on an open ClockEntry anywhere outside GetEmployeeClockEntries's filtered path reproduces the real, unhandled InvalidOperationException -- and because Program.cs has no try/catch, that would terminate the console app. Forgetting using/await using around a SqliteConnection or PayrollDbContext would leave the connection open if an exception occurred mid-method, relying on non-deterministic garbage collection to eventually release it instead of a guaranteed, immediate Dispose call.
summary: GetDuartion's real InvalidOperationException propagates unchanged through PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours and Program.cs, because none of the three catches it -- a real, currently-true fact about this console app, not a hypothetical. using and await using (already at work in the real SQLite integration tests) guarantee Dispose/DisposeAsync runs at the end of a block regardless of whether an exception was thrown inside it, which is exactly why SqliteConnection and DbContext -- both real, external-resource-holding types -- are always opened inside one.
